newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China Grains-Soybeans, meal demand slow, rice drops.
newsitem.headline: China Grains-Soybeans, meal demand slow, rice drops.

text.p: China's soybean and meal demand was freezing up with the approach of the Chinese Lunar New Year in February, but would thaw by April or May, grains and oilseeds traders said on Thursday.
In other grains markets, domestic rice prices were seen dropping and one trader reported Chinese corn exported to central Asia and North Korea. The report could not be confirmed.
"We're waiting for the next campaign, and basically have to wait for April shipment -- that's when South American beans and meal become available again," said one trader.
With heavy arrivals and dwindling demand, the short-term prospect for meal did not look cheery, traders said.
"In (the southern Chinese province of) Guangxi, I hear the ports are getting rather congested, and most of the vessels are carrying meal," said a senior Hong Kong-based oilseeds trader.
With bean prices expected to be more expensive than meal prices, and with China expected to buy more meal than beans in 1997, crushers in China would face difficulties, other traders said.

"If it's beans, we should be talking April, May and June, that's about US$290 per tonne, C&F China, compared to meal, which is at $260 per tonne, C&F China," one Hong Kong-based trader said, noting the $30 spread could hurt crushers.
If crushers imported soybeans, they could not compete with the meal in the domestic market, the trader said.
"Some firms are seriously considering halting work because they make more losses operating than not operating," he said.

U.S. number two soybean was not as attractive to buyers at about $295 per tonne, C&F China, one trader said, noting that some Chinese customers would accept South American soybean at $280 per tonne C&F if the quality was comparable to U.S. beans.
Other traders said the market was waiting for the U.S. Department of Agriculture crop report due later this week.
"If crushing volumes are up, then meal prices might drop and China could buy for forward delivery," the Beijing source said.

Meanwhile, rice prices had dropped across the board on a healthy harvest, Hong Kong and China-based grains traders said. Estmates of the drop varied, with one trader pegging the drop of all categories of rice at about 10 percent since last month.
"For example, the price for wholesale special grade Japonica rice is about 2,800 yuan ($337.35) per tonne, down 10 percent from last month," one trader in the British colony said.

Chinese corn exports were likely in the near term as prices were slowly approaching competitive levels with the international market, traders said, noting that China was keen to export but that buyers were waiting for further price drops.
The price of domestic corn still hovered around 1,050-1,100 yuan per tonne, a China-based grains trader said.
"I think China could export about 200,000 tonnes between January and March," one grains source said, noting he was short and would remain so.
China was already exporting corn to central Asia, another senior trader said, but this report could not be confirmed.

"They are sending corn over there already, and more cargoes are due to head there. It could be a barter deal," the trader said, noting that China had also shipped corn to North Korea, but no details were available.
(US$1 = 8.3 yuan)
-- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6358
